Part 1A brief introduction to Probabilistic Programming in Pyro Draft

Initially the term "probabilistic programming" sounds vague, at least that was my experience. This article was intended as my way to learn the fundamentals of Pyro by documenting my understanding along the process and coming up with examples for myself. Why do we need a programming language for probabilities, can we not just do this in standard languages already? It only started to make sense when I thought about it as a declarative language (think Prolog), that lets you specify probabilistic processes and models and allows you to perform inference and optimization automatically.

In essence, it just gives you the declarative tools for distributions, sampling procedures, evidence etc. and standard tools for optimization, such that you can run arbitrary probabilistic models. In Prolog, we would define facts and rules, in Pyro we define a probabilistic process. Likewise, when running a query in Prolog, the engine performs backtracking automatically (thus inferring the solution). The equivalent in Pyro is the inference via e.g., stochastic variational inference (SVI).

Consider the following example (fictional): You want to infer whether you share a common ancestor with Thomas Bayes. However, you are unsure if your father (William Bayes) is descended from one of Thomas Bayes' brothers, or from another Bayes family. Still, you have estimates for how likely the relationship is: Let’s assume Nathaniel was one of only two men named Bayes of fathering age in the area where William grew up, the other belonging to an unrelated Bayes family. Refer to Figure (a) for an overview.

William naming his eldest son Nathaniel shifts the odds from 1:1 to 1.5:1, giving a 0.6 probability that Nathaniel was William's father. Furthermore, a DNA test shows that you share a stretch of DNA with a known descendant of Joshua Bayes, which happens with probability 0.3 if you are related to him and 0.01 if you are not (for illustration, not realistic). This results in the probabilistic model depicted in (b).

You might define the prolog program as follows to get an answer to your question. Prolog would then backtrack to find you the solution that satisfies all constraints.

Prolog Model
world(nathaniel_bayes).
world(stranger).

parent(_, joshua_bayes, thomas_bayes).
parent(_, joshua_bayes, nathaniel_bayes).
parent(W, W, william).
parent(_, william, you).

ancestor(W, A, X) :- parent(W, A, X).
ancestor(W, A, X) :- parent(W, P, X), ancestor(W, A, P).

related(W, X, Y) :- ancestor(W, A, X), ancestor(W, A, Y).

observed(dna_match).

consistent(W) :- world(W), ( observed(dna_match) -> once(related(W, you, thomas_bayes)) ; true ).

However, as you noticed, in plain prolog, we cannot infer how probable each scenario is exactly, since we can only work with facts. We simply drop the probabilities and treat the DNA match as a hard fact, therefore prolog will respond with W = nathaniel_bayes for the query consistent(W).

In Pyro, we would instead define the probabilistic model below. Here we simply model the generative process by sampling that Nathaniel is William's father with 60% probability. We then say the probability of a match depends on whether Nathaniel is the father (torch.where), using the sampled fact to select this probability. We then provide our observation that there was in fact a DNA-match observed using pyro.sample. Calling model() will result in one sample from the model. The guide here is our current estimate of the posterior, i.e.,

P(Nathaniel is William’s father∣DNA match)P(\text{Nathaniel is William's father} \mid \text{DNA match})P(Nathaniel is William’s father∣DNA match)

Using SVI, we iteratively update the guide to maximize the evidence lower bound (ELBO), which moves it closer to the true posterior. In this example we could calculate the solution analytically, but this is not possible in some complex models. Note that here we explicitly define how we infer our posterior as opposed to implicitly backtracking in Prolog.

Pyro Model
6 import lines
import torch
import pyro
import pyro.distributions as dist
from torch.distributions import constraints
from pyro.infer import SVI, Trace_ELBO
from pyro.optim import Adam

def model():
    nathaniel = pyro.sample("nathaniel_is_father", dist.Bernoulli(0.6))
    p_match = torch.where(nathaniel.bool(), torch.tensor(0.3), torch.tensor(0.01))
    pyro.sample("dna_match", dist.Bernoulli(p_match), obs=torch.tensor(1.0))

def guide():
    q = pyro.param("q", torch.tensor(0.5), constraint=constraints.unit_interval)
    pyro.sample("nathaniel_is_father", dist.Bernoulli(q))

pyro.clear_param_store()
svi = SVI(model, guide, Adam({"lr": 0.01}), Trace_ELBO(max_plate_nesting=0))
for step in range(20_000):
    loss = svi.step()

print(f"P(Nathaniel is father | DNA match) = {pyro.param('q').item():.3f}")
Output
P(Nathaniel is father | DNA match) = 0.985

Although it would be possible to get the exact solution with Pyro, the example shows standard SVI for clarity. Here, we iteratively step towards better posteriors (q) using gradient descent with an Adam optimizer. Due to noisy gradients, our estimate for the posterior will still be an approximation and not exact. However, for reference, we can calculate the exact solution by applying Bayes' rule as follows.

First, we calculate the marginal probability of a match (the evidence) by summing over the hypotheses h∈{Nathaniel,stranger}h \in \{\text{Nathaniel}, \text{stranger}\}h∈{Nathaniel,stranger} for William's father.

P(match)=∑hP(h) P(match∣h)=0.6⋅0.3+0.4⋅0.01=0.184P(\text{match}) = \sum_h P(h)\, P(\text{match} \mid h) = 0.6 \cdot 0.3 + 0.4 \cdot 0.01 = 0.184P(match)=h∑​P(h)P(match∣h)=0.6⋅0.3+0.4⋅0.01=0.184

Then we get the posterior by plugging everything into Bayes' rule.

P(Nathaniel∣match)=P(Nathaniel) P(match∣Nathaniel)P(match)=0.180.184≈0.978.P(\text{Nathaniel} \mid \text{match}) = \frac{P(\text{Nathaniel})\, P(\text{match} \mid \text{Nathaniel})}{P(\text{match})} = \frac{0.18}{0.184} \approx 0.978.P(Nathaniel∣match)=P(match)P(Nathaniel)P(match∣Nathaniel)​=0.1840.18​≈0.978.

We can see that our approximation using SVI is in the ballpark, but not terribly accurate. There would be ways to mitigate this, but we wont consider them here for simplicity. In summary, we can think of Pyro as a declarative language, similar to Prolog, that allows us to reason about uncertainty and gives us tools for inference.

Part 2Stochastic Variational Inference and the Evidence Lower Bound Draft

Integrating is sometimes hard

In order to understand SVI and ELBO we first need to understand why these tools are actually needed. Consider the previous fictional example, we can calculate the posterior easily using the Bayes rule:

P(Nathaniel∣match)=P(Nathaniel) P(match∣Nathaniel)P(match)P(\text{Nathaniel} \mid \text{match}) = \frac{P(\text{Nathaniel})\, P(\text{match} \mid \text{Nathaniel})}{P(\text{match})}P(Nathaniel∣match)=P(match)P(Nathaniel)P(match∣Nathaniel)​

However, let's assume the probability of having a match when Nathaniel is really Williams father depends on the fraction of DNA you actually share with Thomas Bayes, and this fraction depends on the number of generations between you. Let's say the fractions are denoted as aia_iai​ with iii indicating the generations away from Thomas Bayes. Again, this is fictional and only an example that is not realistic. We can write the fractions as a vector:

a=(a1,…,an)\mathbf{a} = (a_1, \dots, a_n)a=(a1​,…,an​)

In our family tree, n=4n = 4n=4 generations separate you from Thomas Bayes (you → William → Nathaniel → Joshua → Thomas).

Further, lets say the aia_iai​ are beta distributed with Beta(α,α)\text{Beta}(\alpha, \alpha)Beta(α,α), an the distribution does not change through time. To calculate P(match∣Nathaniel)P(\text{match} \mid \text{Nathaniel})P(match∣Nathaniel) we now need to integrate over all possible aia_iai​. So the fraction of shared DNA would be s=∏i=1nais = \prod_{i=1}^{n}a_is=∏i=1n​ai​. However, to model the probability of a match given a shared part, we need another function g(⋅)g(\cdot)g(⋅). Using this we can say how fast the probability of a detected match grows with the fraction of shared DNA. A simple choice could be an exponential saturation function g(s)=1−e−k⋅sg(s) = 1 - e^{-k \cdot s}g(s)=1−e−k⋅s as shown below with a parameter kkk that controls how fast we approach a probability of 1. With α=10\alpha = 10α=10 and k≈6k \approx 6k≈6, the average match probability stays at P(match∣Nathaniel)≈0.3P(\text{match} \mid \text{Nathaniel}) \approx 0.3P(match∣Nathaniel)≈0.3, as in the previous article.

If we draw the fractions from a Beta distribution, the probability of an a\mathbf{a}a vector would be:

p(a)=∏i=1nBeta(ai; α,α)p(\mathbf{a}) = \prod_{i=1}^{n} \text{Beta}(a_i;\,\alpha,\alpha)p(a)=i=1∏n​Beta(ai​;α,α)

The probability of a match given Nathaniel is the father and passed on DNA fractions is then:

P(match∣Nathaniel,a)=g(s)P(\text{match} \mid \text{Nathaniel}, \mathbf{a}) = g(s)P(match∣Nathaniel,a)=g(s)

To marginalize out a\mathbf{a}a and get to P(match∣Nathaniel)P(\text{match} \mid \text{Nathaniel})P(match∣Nathaniel) we need to calculate the following integral:

P(match∣Nathaniel)=∫[0,1]np(a)  P(match∣Nathaniel,a)  daP(\text{match} \mid \text{Nathaniel}) = \int_{[0, 1]^n} p(\mathbf{a})\; P(\text{match} \mid \text{Nathaniel}, \mathbf{a})\; d\mathbf{a}P(match∣Nathaniel)=∫[0,1]n​p(a)P(match∣Nathaniel,a)da

Why this is hard: If there is no closed-form solution for an integral, we have to evaluate the function we want to integrate at certain points and then add the slices we get together to approximate the interval. However, if we want to evaluate with the same precision in higher dimensional functions, we need exponentially many evaluations of the function. So if we evaluate m=100m = 100m=100 points for n=10n = 10n=10 generations, we get mn=1020m^n = 10^{20}mn=1020 evaluations, which is not feasible. If we assume our hardware can perform 101110^{11}1011 evaluations per second, it would take us around 32 years for all evaluations.

Stochastic Variational Inference

Now, there is two common ways to model the posterior when we cannot calculate the required probabilities by integration or closed-form. The first is sampling, where we estimate the posterior by sampling parameters for our posterior model (e.g., importance sampling, rejection sampling, MCMC, ...). The second is posing the problem as an optimization and using optimizers to find a good approximation for the posterior (variational inference). We will not go into depth on the difference of these approaches, but generally sampling becomes very expensive with big datasets, since sampled parameters require calculation of the likelihood using the complete dataset. However, there is a trade-off: sampling (MCMC) is asymptotically exact, which is not the case for SVI, but we can estimate gradients using a subset of the data easily, making it more scalable to large datasets.

Evidence Lower Bound

Since we cannot integrate, we need a model of the posterior that we can optimize using some objective. Note that we now have two unobserved (latent) variables: whether Nathaniel is the father and the DNA fractions a\mathbf{a}a. Therefore, we approximate the joint posterior P(Nathaniel,a∣match)P(\text{Nathaniel}, \mathbf{a} \mid \text{match})P(Nathaniel,a∣match) instead of only P(Nathaniel∣match)P(\text{Nathaniel} \mid \text{match})P(Nathaniel∣match). Our estimate for the posterior we will call q(Nathaniel,a)q(\text{Nathaniel}, \mathbf{a})q(Nathaniel,a) from here on out. Let's say we model Nathaniel with a Bernoulli distribution and the fractions aia_iai​ with a single Beta distribution shared across generations, all independent of each other:

q(Nathaniel,a)=Bernoulli(Nathaniel;w)∏i=1nBeta(ai; u,v)q(\text{Nathaniel}, \mathbf{a}) = \text{Bernoulli}(\text{Nathaniel}; w) \prod_{i=1}^{n} \text{Beta}(a_i;\, u, v)q(Nathaniel,a)=Bernoulli(Nathaniel;w)i=1∏n​Beta(ai​;u,v)

Bernoulli(Nathaniel;w)\text{Bernoulli}(\text{Nathaniel}; w)Bernoulli(Nathaniel;w) just states that we evaluate the Bernoulli density at value Nathaniel with the Bernoulli probability www (the parameter of the Bernoulli distribution). Likewise, Beta(ai; u,v)\text{Beta}(a_i;\, u, v)Beta(ai​;u,v) evaluates the Beta density at aia_iai​ with parameters uuu and vvv. The parameters www, uuu and vvv are what we will optimize. In the end, we are mostly interested in Nathaniel, so we approximate the posterior as follows:

P(Nathaniel=1∣match)≈wP(\text{Nathaniel}{=}1 \mid \text{match}) \approx wP(Nathaniel=1∣match)≈w

Now to compare our two distributions, we can use the KL-divergence, which is a distance measure between two probability distributions. In our example, it is defined as:

DKL(q∥P)=Eq[log⁡q(Nathaniel,a)P(Nathaniel,a∣match)]D_\text{KL}\big(q \parallel P\big) = \mathbb{E}_q \left[ \log \frac{q(\text{Nathaniel}, \mathbf{a})}{P(\text{Nathaniel}, \mathbf{a} \mid \text{match})} \right]DKL​(q∥P)=Eq​[logP(Nathaniel,a∣match)q(Nathaniel,a)​]

However, we cannot use this as an objective, since it would require us to calculate P(Nathaniel,a∣match)P(\text{Nathaniel}, \mathbf{a} \mid \text{match})P(Nathaniel,a∣match), which is exactly what we want to approximate:

P(Nathaniel,a∣match)=P(Nathaniel,a,match)∑Nathaniel∫[0,1]nP(Nathaniel,a,match)  daP(\text{Nathaniel}, \mathbf{a} \mid \text{match}) = \frac{P(\text{Nathaniel}, \mathbf{a}, \text{match})}{\sum_{\text{Nathaniel}} \int_{[0, 1]^n} P(\text{Nathaniel}, \mathbf{a}, \text{match})\; d\mathbf{a}}P(Nathaniel,a∣match)=∑Nathaniel​∫[0,1]n​P(Nathaniel,a,match)daP(Nathaniel,a,match)​

Through rearanging the Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence (not shown for simplicity), it can be written as follows:

DKL(q∥P)=Eq[log⁡q(Nathaniel,a)]−Eq[log⁡P(Nathaniel,a,match)]+log⁡P(match)D_\text{KL}\big(q \parallel P\big) = \mathbb{E}_q\big[\log q(\text{Nathaniel}, \mathbf{a})\big] - \mathbb{E}_q\big[\log P(\text{Nathaniel}, \mathbf{a}, \text{match})\big] + \log P(\text{match})DKL​(q∥P)=Eq​[logq(Nathaniel,a)]−Eq​[logP(Nathaniel,a,match)]+logP(match)

This solving for log⁡P(match)\log P(\text{match})logP(match) we get the following:

log⁡P(match)=Eq[log⁡P(Nathaniel,a,match)]−Eq[log⁡q(Nathaniel,a)]⏟ELBO+DKL(q∥P)\log P(\text{match}) = \underbrace{\mathbb{E}_q\big[\log P(\text{Nathaniel}, \mathbf{a}, \text{match})\big] - \mathbb{E}_q\big[\log q(\text{Nathaniel}, \mathbf{a})\big]}_{\text{ELBO}} + D_\text{KL}\big(q \parallel P\big)logP(match)=ELBOEq​[logP(Nathaniel,a,match)]−Eq​[logq(Nathaniel,a)]​​+DKL​(q∥P)

What this means: log⁡P(match)\log P(\text{match})logP(match) does not depend on our approximation of the posterior, so its constant with regard to our optimization. Since it is a sum of the ELBO plus the KL divergence, if the ELBO increases, the KL divergence needs to decrease such that we get the same log⁡P(match)\log P(\text{match})logP(match). Therefore we can simply maximize the ELBO in order to minimize the KL-divergence.

P(Nathaniel∣match)=P(match∣Nathaniel),P(Nathaniel)P(match)P(\text{Nathaniel} \mid \text{match}) = \frac{P(\text{match} \mid \text{Nathaniel}), P(\text{Nathaniel})}{P(\text{match})}P(Nathaniel∣match)=P(match)P(match∣Nathaniel),P(Nathaniel)​

P(match | Nathaniel) is the integral from line 52. To get it, you average over a because you don't know it:

P(match∣Nathaniel)=∫p(a),P(match∣Nathaniel,a),daP(\text{match} \mid \text{Nathaniel}) = \int p(\mathbf{a}), P(\text{match} \mid \text{Nathaniel}, \mathbf{a}), d\mathbf{a}P(match∣Nathaniel)=∫p(a),P(match∣Nathaniel,a),da

Plugging in the two cases

  • Nathaniel=0: P(match | 0, a) = 0.01 for every a, so the integral is just 0.01. Nothing hard here.
  • Nathaniel=1: P(match | 1, a) = g(s), which depends on a. Write I = ∫ p(a) g(s) da. This is the n-dimensional integral that's hard to compute.

Then:

P(Nathaniel=1∣match)=P(1),IP(1),I+P(0)⋅0.01P(\text{Nathaniel}{=}1 \mid \text{match}) = \frac{P(1), I}{P(1), I + P(0)\cdot 0.01}P(Nathaniel=1∣match)=P(1),I+P(0)⋅0.01P(1),I​
